label: Affine Geometry
notes: Chapter 13 spans printed pages 191 to 228 and isolates the geometry of incidence and parallelism. We keep collinearity, betweenness, ratios along a line, and area ratios, but deliberately forget Euclidean length and angle. This forgetting is the organizing idea behind every result that follows.

label: What Affine Geometry Keeps
notes: The affine dictionary separates what survives an arbitrary affinity from what does not. Incidence, parallelism, division ratios, and signed area ratios persist; distances, angles, and circularity vanish. Knowing which column a statement lives in tells you whether it is genuinely an affine theorem worth proving here.

label: Parallel Axiom and Pencils
notes: Through a point off a line there is exactly one parallel, so parallelism becomes an equivalence relation that sorts every line into a pencil sharing one direction. This single axiom replaces the Euclidean metric scaffolding and lets us reason about whole families of lines at once rather than individual segments.

label: The Desargues Axiom
notes: The affine Desargues axiom controls triangles whose corresponding sides are parallel. Either the three connecting lines meet at one center, giving a central dilatation, or they form a parallel pencil, giving a translation. This dichotomy is the engine that makes dilatations well defined throughout the chapter.

label: Parallel Projection Preserves Ratio
notes: Project one line onto another by a family of parallel lines. Lengths and angles distort, yet the ratio in which a point divides a segment is carried across unchanged. This invariance of division ratio is the cornerstone affine fact, and every later result on midpoints and centroids rests on it.

label: Dilatations and Translations
notes: A dilatation sends every line to a parallel line. When the connecting lines share a finite center it is a central dilatation scaling by a factor k; when they are parallel it is a translation with no fixed point. Half-turns are the special dilatations of factor minus one that interchange two points.

label: Vectors as Translations
notes: An ordered pair of points names the translation that carries the first to the second, and composing translations adds these vectors. Because translation composition is commutative, the translations form an Abelian group. Vector addition, midpoints, and parallelograms thus emerge from affine structure alone, with no appeal to length or angle.

label: Affinities
notes: An affinity is any invertible map x maps to Ax plus b with A nonsingular. It preserves collinearity, parallelism, and division ratios along every line, so it is exactly the symmetry group of affine geometry. The fundamental theorem states the converse: any collineation preserving parallelism is such an affine map.

label: Equiaffinities and Area
notes: An affinity multiplies every signed area by the determinant of A. When the determinant equals one the map is an equiaffinity, and area becomes its natural invariant even though the figure is sheared or stretched. The shear family illustrates this: the triangle deforms continuously while its signed area stays exactly fixed.

label: Dividing a Segment
notes: A point P on segment AB is fixed by the ratio AP to PB, written as a signed value. Affinities and parallel projections preserve this ratio, so the midpoint, the points of trisection, and any internal division are affine notions. This signed ratio is the algebraic quantity that all subsequent theorems manipulate.

label: Ceva's Theorem
notes: For cevians from the vertices of a triangle through a common point, the three division ratios on the sides multiply to plus one. Concurrence is an affine condition because it involves only ratios along lines, so Ceva's theorem belongs entirely to affine geometry and needs no measurement of length or angle.

label: Menelaus and the Centroid
notes: Menelaus' theorem gives the dual: collinear points on the three sides yield a ratio product of minus one. Setting all cevian ratios to one recovers the medians, whose intersection is the centroid dividing each median two to one. The medial triangle and centroid are pure affine consequences of these ratio laws.

label: Barycentric Coordinates
notes: Masses placed at the three vertices determine a balance point, and after normalization the coordinates are the signed area shares of the opposite subtriangles. Because they are origin independent weighted averages, barycentric coordinates convert lines, cevians, and transversals into clean determinant conditions encompassing both Ceva and Menelaus at once.

label: Conics and the Line at Infinity
notes: Adjoining the line at infinity lets us classify conics affinely by how they meet it. An ellipse misses the line, a parabola touches it once, and a hyperbola crosses it twice. This single incidence test distinguishes the three nondegenerate conics without any reference to foci, eccentricity, or distance.
